newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-British Steel says stg hurting margins.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-British Steel says stg hurting margins.

text.p: British Steel warned on Wednesday that sterling's irrepressible rise was continuing to squeeze its profit margins, harming not just its own profitability but that of many of its customers.
As sterling moved comfortably above the crucial three Deutsche mark level in recent days, the steel giant made its strongest comments yet on the need for action by the British government.
The British pound has soared by 35 percent since last August and is now at its highest level since 1989.

Brian Moffat, chairman and chief executive, told the British Steel annual meeting that despite maintaining "cautious optimism" about the outlook "the pound has continued to strengthen, particularly against the Deutsche mark".

"Inevitably this has led to our profit margins coming under increasing pressure. Similarly, sterling's strength will be seriously impairing the competitiveness of many of our UK customers, particularly those who are significant exporters."
British Steel is unusually exposed to the currency movements because 85 percent of its sales are mark-sensitive and 55 percent of its sales are for export.

All sales on the continent are priced in marks and the group has faced the double-whammy of being undercut by competitors on the continent and having their cheap steel exports undermining its sales in British Steel's home market too.
Last month British Steel reported a collapse in annual profits to 451 million pounds ($758.1 million) from 1.1 billion the year before.
As a result, the group implemented a rolling cost cutting and job reduction programme starting with 2,000 redundancies this year.
But Moffat said Britain's July 2 budget had made its turnaround task even harder.

"It is particularly disappointing that since the Budget the pound has shown an even stronger upward trend and has risen by some 13 pfennigs from a level that had already undermined our competitive position."

British Steel thinks it is unlikely the pound will weaken, with the market predicting further British interest rate hikes to cool the consumer boom which was seen to be largely untouched by the budget measures.
Moffat criticised the focus on monetary tightening to curb inflation, rather than using fiscal measures in tandem.

He said it was "unrealistic to put virtually all the pressure for these actions (to control inflation) on interest rates when governments of other European members states are using fiscal policy rather than interest rates."
Just a few months ago the steel group believed the likelihood of the pound moving over three marks was minimal.
Moffat told shareholders the company's dollar-denominated business was unscathed, but business in Europe had been hit hard.
Firmer European steel prices only partly mitigated the impact of sterling, he said.

As a result, British Steel shares have significantly underperformed the FTSE 100 index by 32 percent over the last year according to Reuters 3000 data, with the deterioration setting in at the close of 1996 when the sterling problem became apparent.
Moffat said the poor value had triggered the 145 million pounds share buyback last week.

The group renewed shareholder permission to buy a further 10 percent of shares this year. But Moffat refused to comment on whether the power would be utilised. British Steel had around 785 million in cash before buying up its shares last week.
The outlook for profits in the current financial year remains bleak, with analysts' forecasts mostly ranging between 100 and 200 million pounds in pretax profits, but UBS predicting a loss.
If UBS is right British Steel will have collapsed into the red from a 1.1 billion profit within just two years.
($ = 0.594 British Pounds)
